, was taken from the J language, which originated the concept. Tacit code can be made super-terse, and is best reserved for short snippets only. APL
-- short, efficient, and ultra-optimised bits of code, are often expressed in tacit. You’ll find that pretty much everything on
is written in tacit, and as you start working on improving your
handicap, tacit is an essential skill.

We can look at tacit programming in APL as a little embedded DSL for functional composition, complete with its own grammar. The rules of this grammar are actually quite simple, but learning how to read and write tacit functions takes a lot of practice, even for those well-versed in the rest of APL.
means implicit, and refers to a function where there is no explicit mention of its arguments. In a tacit function, then, you’ll see no
as you would in a dfn. Instead a set of rules decide how the components of a tacit function interact with the arguments.

(also known as a 3-train) -- a tacit combination of
X (f g h) Y → (X f Y) g (X h Y)
This is perhaps the simplest tacit rule that one can see applications for. Consider the three-way compare (sometimes called “spaceship”) operator,

that some languages (like Perl or Ruby) offer. It returns a negative value if a < b, 0 if a == b and a positive value if a > b. APL has no such thing, but we can cook up a tacit function using the fork rule:
Let’s look at the rule application to see why it works:
(a > b) - (a < b) ⍝ using the fork rule: (X f Y) g (X h Y)
Once you learn to see this pattern, it really crops up frequently. Why is it called a “fork”? Well, if we have specified

That last example -- a monadic fork -- can be formalised as:
There are, in fact, two more fork-varieties, beyond the two we’ve already seen. They differ in how the consitutent functions are applied (monadically or dyadically):

X(Z g h)Y → Z g X h Y ⍝ h dyad, g dyad, derived dyad
(X g h)Y  → X g h Y   ⍝ h modad, g dyad, derived monad

This is where the real fun begins. We can string together longer tacit functions by combining forks and atops. Some consideration should be given to comprehensibility here. Long stretches of tacit code requires more effort to understand than the corresponding explicit formulation.
As our tacit rules indicate, barring the presence of parentheses, a combination of three functions is a fork, and two functions is an atop. If we have
than three functions, we start reading from the right, making groups of threes and twos, and combine
using the fork and atop rules.
...in the absence of parentheses, a sequence of an odd number of functions resolves to a 3-train (fork) and an even-numbered sequence resolves to a 2-train (atop)
